Hahah, yeah sorry. I can see it being interpreted that way. Let me explain my position.

There was a time, not that long ago in the grand scheme of things, where it would have been all but impossible for you to ever earn money - let alone own land. You would expected to work, for the rest of your life, on the land of a lord just to repay the graciousness of that lord for granting you the ability to stay on his land. You'd receive no pay or remuneration aside from the 'privilege' of being able to take from all the food you produced, enough for your family to survive. It's just the way things were. This system and similar systems lasted for thousands of years - many times longer than capitalism or even capitalism and mercantalism combined have been around. Expecting a lord to pay you, just for services rendered, would be an absurd level of entitlement. Why should he pay you to work his land when there are countless people who'd love to have the right just to work his land so they can survive? We've come an enormous way since then, but I think we still have much further to go.

Automation is going to be what sparks the next economic transition. I believe we're going to stay in a heavily merit based society, but work will in time come to be an option. There are a lot of ways to go about this, but what I would prefer consider are the impacts of this change. For instance petty need-based property crime would all but disappear. We'd also have, for the first time ever, a true free market of labor pricing. In the US for instance a working class individual can not say no to an employer. Jobs are hard to come by (as everybody needs one and there are far fewer jobs than people that need jobs) and an employer can exploit this disparity by setting his labor price as low as legally possible. If there was no minimum wage in the US WalMart would still be able to fill their job openings if they paid in rice, water, and bread instead of money. That is not a free market of labor. People need to live and are thus forced to accept whatever wage offered for the most part. In countries like Denmark, Norway, Finland, Sweden, etc there are no minimum wages. Instead they have strong unions that collectively negotiate each year for prices on the workers' behalves but again having somebody else negotiate for you isn't exactly free market. When work is optional and workers can afford to say no, suddenly labor prices would reach their true equilibrium.

Work quality would also improve. Right now I think the current coercive system we use for employment creates mutual animosity. Workers hate their job and frequently also have no good will towards their employer either. They don't want to be there, they're not getting paid what they consider a fair salary, and so on. The employer in turn responds to this by also starting to dehumanize his workers. It's no longer Joe in accounting, it's your human resources assigned accountant who can be restructured or made redundant as necessary. Have your "human resources" train their own cheaper replacements from India before making them "redundant"? Sure, why not - they're not actual people after all.. just resources to be exploited as profits dictate.

There's also psychological issues. Things like IQ have actually been shown to vary dynamically based on your present living conditions. People literally do not think as well when under financial duress, as I think people who have been there can attest to. This was able to be tested in India where farmers receive insufficient funds to live for an entire year, but they receive the majority of their annual earnings in one lump sum at harvest time. Thus during the first part of the year they can live quite comfortably, but as the months stretch on they enter into more and more dire straights until harvest time when the process cycles once again.

Of course I have no illusions we're not going go from today to the rather pleasant scenario I'm describing. It will be gradual and we're likely not going to change even when it's absolutely necessary, but some years after that as we resort to increasingly bandages to try to keep our currently system alive (think recently about US government officials arguing that driverless vehicles still must have a functional steering wheel and other vehicular ornamentation). Regardless, though I am far from Machiavellian - starting the transition towards the future is something I will rejoice and fully support every time in the name of the long term good, even if I do realize it's going to result in some short term suffering.
